title: Steering Vectors are an Adversarial Attack Surface

paper.title: Steering Vectors are an Adversarial Attack Surface
paper.abstract: Abstract Activation steering has become a popular way to control Large Language Model (LLM) behavior without fine-tuning. Since the technique is plug-and-play, users share datasets and precomputed vectors to steer model activations. However, we show that a stealth data poisoning attack silently compromises this pipeline. By substituting 4 − 6 % 4{-}6\% of tokens in the steering dataset, an attacker can silently align the resulting vector with an anti-refusal direction. This jailbreaks the target model while preserving the intended steering effect on benign prompts. Under this threat model, a malicious actor can distribute an apparently safe bundle containing texts, vectors, and weights, alongside an equivalence certificate that the end-user can verify. We test the attack on two open-weight model families and eight model-attribute combinations, observing that poisoned vectors reach an absolute attack success rate (ASR) of 20 − 55 % 20{-}55\% , + 19 % +19\% to + 51 % +51\% over a clean reference. Finally, we find that a refusal-direction orthogonalization defense can recover ≈ 82 % {\approx}82\% of the ASR gap without harming benign behavior. AbzalAidakhmetov/adversarial_attack

Large language models (LLMs) undergo extensive safety alignment to refuse harmful requests, yet adversarial jailbreaks remain a persistent threat. Most existing attacks operate at the prompt level : gradient-based adversarial suffixes ( Zou et al., 2023 ) , automated red-teaming ( Chao et al., 2025 ) , or template-based injections ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Wei et al., 2023 ) . These approaches are visible in the model input and increasingly mitigated by perplexity-based or classifier-based input filters. In parallel, a different paradigm for controlling LLM behavior has gained traction: activation steering ( Turner et al., 2024 ; Zou et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2023 ) . Rather than crafting adversarial prompts, users compute a direction vector from contrastive text pairs, prompts that exhibit a target attribute ( pos ) versus prompts that do not ( neg ), and add this vector to the model’s hidden states at inference time. The technique is simple, requires no fine-tuning, and generalizes across open-weight models ( Rimsky et al., 2024 ) . Because it is lightweight and reusable, activation steering enables a new ecosystem of shared steering datasets and precomputed vectors , in which users have the possibility to download and apply steering artifacts computed by others rather than recomputing them in-house ( Appendix C ).

sections.heading: A supply-chain vulnerability.
sections.text: This sharing practice introduces a new trust surface. If a user computes a steering vector from a community-provided contrastive dataset, nothing prevents a malicious contributor from poisoning that dataset. We show that such poisoning can be both effective and stealthy : the attacker makes small token substitutions in the contrastive pair texts, constrained to embedding-space nearest neighbors, so that the resulting steering vector silently aligns with the anti-refusal direction . When applied at inference, the poisoned vector suppresses the model’s safety guardrails. A user who downloads a dataset labeled “bullet list formatting” would unwittingly deploy a jailbreak vector. Crucially, the vulnerability survives strong provenance guarantees: even if the attacker ships a bundle (pair texts, precomputed vector, suggested weight) together with a cryptographic equivalence certificate that the user can re-derive locally, the certificate proves only that the vector was computed correctly from the released texts, and it is the texts that carry the payload. The attack therefore targets a regime that bit-exact reproducibility does not defend against.

sections.heading: Why this is possible.
sections.text: The attack exploits a fundamental property of LLM representations: entanglement . The direction encoding a benign attribute (e.g., “use bullet lists”) occupies the same space as the direction mediating refusal ( Arditi et al., 2024 ) ; there is no orthogonality guarantee between them, so small perturbations to the contrastive texts can rotate the steering vector toward 𝐫 \mathbf{r} . Because the vector is a mean-difference of hidden states, each token substitution contributes a small Δ \Delta , and gradient-guided search lets these deltas accumulate into a significant directional shift while each individual change remains imperceptible.

sections.heading: What distinguishes our attack.
sections.text: Our approach differs from prior work along three axes. Attack surface: we target the steering dataset , not the inference-time prompt; the adversarial payload is baked into the contrastive pairs before any user touches the model. Stealth: unlike GCG-style suffixes that produce gibberish (perplexity > 1000 {>}1000 ), our replacements are constrained to embedding-space nearest neighbours from a curated safe vocabulary and are dominantly synonym-like swaps ( write → \to describe , short → \to concise , poem → \to poetry ); the optimiser typically modifies only 4–6% of tokens, and the resulting vector still elicits the declared attribute on benign prompts essentially as strongly as the clean vector, with ℓ 2 \ell_{2} norm essentially unchanged on seven of eight combos. Mechanism: the attack manipulates neither model weights, as in training-data poisoning ( Carlini et al., 2024 ; Wan et al., 2023 ) , nor the input, but corrupts a post-hoc representation-level intervention, bypassing both input filters and weight-level audits.

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: 1. We identify contrastive steering datasets as a novel attack surface and formalise the supply-chain threat model ( Section 3 ). 2. We propose a GCG-style optimisation constrained to embedding-space neighbours with fluency penalties and safe-vocabulary filtering, producing stealthy poisoned contrastive pairs ( Section 3 ). 3. We validate the attack on two open-weight model families and eight model–attribute combos spanning language, formatting, and case, showing 0.20 0.20 – 0.55 0.55 ASR ( + 19 +19 to + 51 +51 pp over clean) while leaving the declared steering effect on benign prompts and the vector’s ℓ 2 \ell_{2} norm essentially unchanged on seven of eight combos ( Section 4 ).

sections.heading: Activation steering and representation engineering.
sections.text: Turner et al. (2024) introduced Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA): computing mean-difference vectors from contrastive text pairs and adding them to hidden states to steer model behavior. Zou et al. (2025) generalized this into Representation Engineering, a framework for reading and controlling model internals via linear probes and interventions. Rimsky et al. (2024) demonstrated contrastive steering on Llama 2 across a range of behavioral attributes, and Li et al. (2023) applied similar interventions to elicit truthful outputs. Arditi et al. (2024) showed that refusal in LLMs is mediated by a single linear direction, and that ablating this direction eliminates refusal entirely. These works establish the techniques we build on, and the assumptions we exploit. None consider the security of the contrastive dataset used to compute steering vectors.

sections.heading: Adversarial attacks on LLMs.
sections.text: Zou et al. (2023) proposed Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG), a gradient-based method that appends adversarial suffixes to prompts, achieving transferable jailbreaks. GCG produces high-perplexity gibberish that is detectable by input filters. Liu et al. (2024) developed AutoDAN, which uses evolutionary search to produce more readable adversarial prompts, and Chao et al. (2025) introduced PAIR, leveraging an attacker LLM to iteratively refine jailbreak prompts. Wei et al. (2023) taxonomized failure modes of LLM safety training, including competing objectives and mismatched generalization. All of these attacks operate at the prompt level at inference time. Our attack is fundamentally different: it corrupts the steering dataset before inference, so the adversarial prompts at test time are clean, unmodified harmful requests.

sections.heading: Data poisoning and backdoor attacks.
sections.text: Carlini et al. (2024) demonstrated that poisoning web-scale training datasets is practical. Wan et al. (2023) showed that instruction-tuning data can be poisoned to degrade model safety. Hubinger et al. (2024) trained deceptive “sleeper agent” models that persist through safety training. These attacks target model weights via the training pipeline. Our attack targets a post-hoc representation-level intervention : the model weights are never modified, and the poisoning operates on an auxiliary dataset used solely for steering vector computation. This makes our threat model orthogonal to classical data poisoning.

sections.heading: 3.1 Threat Model
sections.text: We consider an attacker with white-box access to the target model, realistic for open-weight models such as Gemma ( Gemma Team, 2024 ) and Llama ( Llama Team, AI @ Meta, 2024 ) , who distributes a bundle : contrastive pair texts, a precomputed steering vector 𝐯 \mathbf{v} , a recommended steering weight α \alpha , and an equivalence certificate the user can verify by re-deriving 𝐯 \mathbf{v} from the released texts. A user who downloads the bundle (i) re-derives 𝐯 \mathbf{v} to confirm provenance, (ii) reads the pair texts to check they look natural, and (iii) runs a benign sanity check that ( 𝐯 , α ) (\mathbf{v},\alpha) produces the advertised attribute behaviour, and if all three pass deploys at the bundled α \alpha . The cryptographic certificate proves only that 𝐯 \mathbf{v} was correctly computed from the released texts; it does not detect that the texts themselves carry the payload. The attacker’s goal is to modify the dataset so that the resulting steering vector aligns with 𝐫 \mathbf{r} , the anti-refusal direction, suppressing safety guardrails at inference. The attack is subject to a stealth constraint : the poisoned texts must be plausible paraphrases of the originals. We enforce this through (i) a per-text edit budget of at most n mod n_{\text{mod}} token changes, (ii) replacements restricted to embedding-space nearest neighbors, (iii) replacements drawn from a curated safe vocabulary, and (iv) a hard perplexity cap on modified texts.

After removing terms flagged by Detoxify ( Hanu and Unitary team, 2020 ) , and by a Llama-3.3-70B safety screen, we keep only single-token subword-complete entries beginning with a space. This yields ∼ 36 {\sim}36 K safe tokens for Gemma-2 and ∼ 14.6 {\sim}14.6 K for Llama; full pipeline in Appendix A . sections.heading: 3.4 Optimization
sections.text: We adapt the Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) framework ( Zou et al., 2023 ) to our constrained setting. The key differences from standard GCG are: (i) candidates are drawn from embedding neighbors rather than the full vocabulary, (ii) a per-text edit budget is strictly enforced, (iii) both pos and neg texts are modified, and (iv) fluency penalties are incorporated into candidate scoring.

sections.heading: Early stopping.
sections.text: The optimizer is run for at most B B iterations and stopped earlier if no sampled candidate edit is accepted for P P consecutive iterations. A candidate edit is accepted only when its objective value is higher than that of the current dataset. The values of B B and P P used in our experiments are reported in Section 4 . Appendix K formalizes these progress and termination properties for the implemented sampled algorithm: accepted updates preserve the edit constraints, strictly improve the objective, and the stated stopping rules ensure finite termination.

sections.heading: Suffix protection.
sections.text: The instruction suffix that defines the steering attribute (e.g., "Your answer should contain exactly 3 bullet points" ) is identified via character-level boundary detection and excluded from modification . This ensures the poisoned dataset still appears to target the claimed attribute, maintaining the social engineering aspect of the attack. Algorithm 1 (in Appendix A ) summarizes the complete attack pipeline.

sections.heading: Models.
sections.text: We evaluate on two open-weight instruction-tuned models spanning different families and scales: Gemma-2-2B-IT ( Gemma Team, 2024 ) at layer 14 and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct ( Llama Team, AI @ Meta, 2024 ) at layer 18. We selected these layers using a preliminary coarse sweep over candidate layers, choosing layers that produced reliable steering for the target attribute. Models are loaded in bfloat16 .

sections.heading: Steering attributes.
sections.text: For each model we select attributes that span three classes of behaviour (language, formatting, and case) and that admit a programmatic compliance check: spanish , french , lowercase , and has_bold_only on both Gemma-2-2B and Llama-3.1-8B (eight model–attribute combos total). For each combo we use N = 20 N{=}20 contrastive pairs. pos texts contain the attribute instruction suffix (e.g. ‘‘...write your response in all lowercase letters.’’ ); neg texts are the same prompts with the suffix removed. The attribute-specifying span of each pos text is identified by per-row substring matching and excluded from modification ( Section 3.4 ), so the poisoned dataset still appears to target the claimed attribute.

sections.heading: Attack configuration.
sections.text: We use n mod = 5 n_{\text{mod}}=5 (max tokens modified per text), K = 100 K{=}100 embedding neighbors, λ lm = 0.2 \lambda_{\text{lm}}{=}0.2 , perplexity cap τ = 2000 \tau{=}2000 , and C = 64 C{=}64 candidates per iteration. The GCG budget is B = 1500 B{=}1500 iterations with patience P = 500 P{=}500 for both model sizes. Each (model, attribute) combo is attacked with three independent GCG seeds ( s ∈ { 0 , 1 , 2 } s\in\{0,1,2\} ); all reported metrics are the mean over seeds, and we annotate ± 1 \pm 1 standard deviation across seeds wherever the quantity depends on the poisoned vector. The clean steering vector is computed deterministically from the unmodified pair texts and therefore has no per-seed dispersion.

sections.heading: Evaluation.
sections.text: We report two metrics on disjoint 100-prompt evaluation sets (no overlap with the harmful/harmless splits used to estimate 𝐫 \mathbf{r} ). ASR (attack success rate) is the fraction of harmful -prompt responses that a three-judge ensemble ( Claude-Sonnet-4.5 , GPT-4.1 , and Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct , all prompted with the same rubric and instructed to mark looping, incoherent, or off-topic outputs as safe) flags as jailbroken by majority vote; Appendix F reports the inter-judge agreement (Fleiss’ κ F = 0.91 \kappa_{F}=0.91 ). AC (Attribute Compliance) is the fraction of harmless -prompt responses that satisfy the attribute’s predicate: for lowercase and has_bold_only this is a deterministic regex; for spanish / french it is an off-the-shelf language-ID confidence test 1 1 1 fastText’s lid.176 model ( Joulin et al., 2016 ; Joulin et al., 2017 ) . ( p lang ≥ 0.5 p_{\text{lang}}\geq 0.5 ) with a 40-character floor to discard noisy short outputs. Steering is applied during the prompt prefill pass only; see Appendix B for the all-step variant.

sections.heading: Weight selection.
sections.text: Under the bundle threat model of Section 3 , the attacker controls α \alpha and picks the value that maximises poisoned ASR subject to the bundle remaining plausible (non-degenerate clean-vector AC, perplexity in the normal range). For each combo we evaluate at the attacker-rational integer α ∈ { 2 , 3 , 4 } \alpha\in\{2,3,4\} ; per-combo weights are reported in Table 2 . Our headline metric is absolute ASR at the bundled α \alpha ; clean-vector ASR at the same α \alpha is the counterfactual reference, and we refer to the difference as Δ \Delta ASR.

sections.heading: Attribute retention on benign prompts.
sections.text: This is the stealth result. On six of the eight combos, the poisoned steering vector continues to elicit the declared attribute on benign prompts at a rate within ± 0.07 \pm 0.07 of the clean vector. The largest absolute AC changes are Gemma spanish ( + 0.11 +0.11 ) and Llama lowercase ( + 0.08 +0.08 ), both lifts : a benign user sanity-checking the poisoned vector sees the declared attribute fire more reliably, not less. The remaining combos are essentially flat (Llama french 0.00 0.00 , Llama spanish − 0.01 -0.01 , Gemma lowercase − 0.02 -0.02 , Gemma has_bold_only + 0.01 +0.01 ) and stay at ≥ 0.58 \geq 0.58 absolute on the six combos with a working clean-vector attribute, with per-seed std ≤ 0.04 \text{std}\leq 0.04 throughout. Gemma lowercase is an outlier in the opposite direction: even the clean vector achieves only AC = 0.14 =0.14 at the bundled weight (the lowercase attribute is weakly represented at layer 14 on Gemma-2B), so the attribute sanity check at step (iii) of the bundle protocol would alert a careful defender that the vector does not reliably do its declared job, irrespective of any attack. For the seven well-behaved combos, a user who downloads a community-provided “Spanish-output”, “French-output”, “lowercase-output”, or “bold-only” bundle and sanity-checks it on benign prompts will see exactly what they expect: the vector reliably produces the declared behaviour. The jailbreak payload manifests only when the same vector is applied to a harmful prompt. The combination of the two columns is the threat: a vector that visibly does its declared job on benign inputs is unlikely to be discarded by a casual user, yet flips refusals on harmful inputs at a rate of 0.20 0.20 – 0.55 0.55 , a ratio of 2 2 – 20 × 20\times the clean-vector counterfactual’s depending on the combo.

sections.heading: 4.4 Directional Specificity
sections.text: A natural concern is that the attack might be a norm-inflation artefact. Appendix D ( Figure 5 ) shows this is not the case: on seven of eight combos the poisoned-to-clean ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm ratio sits in [ 0.96 , 1.20 ] [0.96,1.20] (four below 1.0 1.0 ); the single outlier (Llama has_bold_only at 1.78 × 1.78\times ) is driven by an unusually small clean-vector norm. Removing it, ASR still rises sharply across the remaining seven, so the lift is not explainable by larger vectors at the same weight: the cosine rotation toward 𝐫 \mathbf{r} in Figure 3 is the dominant driver. GPT-2 perplexity on benign responses also stays in the same range under both vectors.

sections.heading: 4.5 Text Naturalness
sections.text: The optimiser edits on average 120 120 tokens per combo across seeds (std ≤ 10 \leq 10 ), ≈ 6 % \approx 6\% of modifiable tokens (per-text budget n mod = 5 n_{\text{mod}}=5 , worst case 200 200 per combo). The dominant pattern is synonym-like substitution: representative swaps from the Gemma spanish run include write → \to describe , letter → \to message , poem → \to poetry , short → \to concise . A minority of swaps are noisier: examples are entity shifts like Japan → \to China , some POS-changing morphological cousins ( photosynthesis → \to photosynthetic ), or near-homophones ( recipe → \to receipt ). By contrast GCG-style adversarial suffixes produce perplexity > 1000 {>}1000 and visibly random tokens; here, the modified texts read as plausible paraphrases.

sections.heading: 4.7 Refusal-Direction Orthogonalisation
sections.text: A natural mitigation for a defender with access to harmful/harmless prompts is to sanitise an untrusted steering vector by projecting the refusal direction out of it: 𝐯 def = 𝐯 − ( 𝐯 ⋅ 𝐫 ^ ) ​ 𝐫 ^ \mathbf{v}_{\text{def}}=\mathbf{v}-(\mathbf{v}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{r}})\hat{\mathbf{r}} . By construction cos ⁡ ( 𝐯 def , 𝐫 ) = 0 \cos(\mathbf{v}_{\text{def}},\mathbf{r})=0 , while the orthogonal component on which the declared attribute almost entirely relies ( Figure 3 ) is preserved. Figure 4 reports the per-combo breakdown. The orthogonalisation reduces poisoned-vector ASR by 0.09 0.09 – 0.51 0.51 absolute (mean − 0.27 -0.27 ), recovering on average 82 % 82\% of the gap between the poisoned and clean ASR, staying at or below the baseline on three combos. Harmless-prompt AC changes by at most ± 0.09 \pm 0.09 on all eight combos (defended vs. poisoned); the mean change is essentially zero, and for Llama spanish the defended AC actually rises ( 0.84 → 0.88 0.84\to 0.88 ). On the clean-vector control the defense is a near-no-op ( | Δ ​ ASR | ≤ 0.05 |\Delta\text{ASR}|\leq 0.05 and | Δ ​ AC | ≤ 0.02 |\Delta\text{AC}|\leq 0.02 on the seven well-behaved combos), consistent with | cos ⁡ ( 𝐯 clean , 𝐫 ) | ≤ 0.10 |\cos(\mathbf{v}_{\text{clean}},\mathbf{r})|\leq 0.10 from Figure 3 . The defense works precisely because the attack relies on a large 𝐯 ⋅ 𝐫 \mathbf{v}{\cdot}\mathbf{r} component: by Figure 3 the poisoned vectors sit at mean cos ⁡ ( 𝐯 , 𝐫 ) ∈ [ 0.22 , 0.59 ] \cos(\mathbf{v},\mathbf{r})\in[0.22,0.59] , and zeroing out that component absorbs most of the jailbreak lift while sparing the attribute-bearing orthogonal component. The defense neutralises the attack of Section 3 as written; an adaptive attacker can co-optimise under a hard cap cos ⁡ ( 𝐯 , 𝐫 ) ≤ τ \cos(\mathbf{v},\mathbf{r})\leq\tau to stay below the defender’s threshold. We sweep this cap on the strongest Llama combo in Appendix E and find that the threshold defense remains robust: on Llama lowercase , at τ = 0.10 \tau=0.10 the constrained attacker recovers only 3 % 3\% of the unconstrained ASR gap (and ≤ 9 % {\leq}9\% across τ ∈ [ 0.05 , 0.30 ] \tau\in[0.05,0.30] ).

sections.heading: 5 Conclusions
sections.text: We demonstrated that contrastive activation steering datasets can be stealthily poisoned to produce jailbreak vectors, even when the attacker ships a complete bundle (texts + vector + weight + equivalence certificate) and the user verifies provenance. Constraining replacements to embedding-space neighbours from a curated safe vocabulary generates texts that look like minor paraphrases, with the optimiser typically touching only 4–6% of modifiable tokens. Across two model families and eight combinations, poisoned vectors reach 0.20 0.20 – 0.55 0.55 absolute ASR ( + 19 +19 to + 51 +51 pp over the clean counterfactual) while attribute compliance on benign prompts shifts by at most 0.11 0.11 and ℓ 2 \ell_{2} norm stays close to clean on seven of eight combos, so a user who sanity-checks the bundled artefact sees the behaviour the dataset’s label promises, and the jailbreak surfaces only on harmful inputs. Verification of shared steering artefacts must therefore test the artefact on adversarial inputs, not just on the benign queries it was advertised to steer, and not only by re-deriving the vector from the texts.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: The attack requires white-box access for gradient computation and embedding-neighbour lookup; this is realistic for open-weight models but does not apply to closed APIs. We test only up to 8B parameters; larger models may have different representational geometry both for 𝐫 \mathbf{r} and for the entanglement we exploit. One combo (Gemma-2-2B lowercase at layer 14) is weakly-steered (clean AC = 0.14 =0.14 at the bundled weight), failing the bundle protocol’s benign sanity check; we retain it for transparency but it does not contribute to the stealth claim. Finally, we only target the refusal direction; other attack objectives and cross-model transferability remain unexplored.

sections.heading: Safe vocabulary pipeline.
sections.text: We construct the safe vocabulary mask over the model’s tokenizer via the following pipeline: 1. Start from the NLTK English word corpus ( ∼ 234 {\sim}234 K words). 2. Remove words flagged as toxic by Detoxify ( Hanu and Unitary team, 2020 ) . 3. Remove words flagged by Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct screening. 4. Map surviving words to the model’s tokenizer vocabulary, keeping only single-token entries that begin with a space character (i.e., subword-complete tokens). This yields approximately 36K safe tokens for Gemma-2 and 14.6K for the Llama tokenizer.

sections.heading: Appendix C Realized Attack Surface
sections.text: The sharing pipeline our threat model targets is not hypothetical: steering artifacts are already distributed and deployed today. Control vectors are a first-class inference feature in llama.cpp , 2 2 2 https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/5970 where a user can apply a downloaded vector via a single --control-vector flag. Pre-computed vectors for popular open-weight models (Llama-3, Mistral-Large, Mixtral, Qwen-1.5, miqu) are distributed on the HuggingFace Hub as ready-to-load artifacts, 3 3 3 https://huggingface.co/jukofyork/creative-writing-control-vectors-v3.0 , 4 4 4 https://huggingface.co/datasets/codelion/Qwen3-0.6B-pts-steering-vectors alongside benchmark suites for evaluating shared steering methods. 5 5 5 https://huggingface.co/datasets/WangResearchLab/SteeringSafety Python libraries that wrap the train–share–apply workflow ( repeng 6 6 6 https://github.com/vgel/repeng and steering-vectors 7 7 7 https://github.com/steering-vectors/steering-vectors ) are publicly available on PyPI and import directly from HuggingFace model and dataset identifiers. At the commercial end, Goodfire’s Ember API hosts feature-level steering as a paid service backed by open-sourced sparse autoencoders for Llama-3.1-8B and Llama-3.3-70B. 8 8 8 https://www.goodfire.ai/blog/sae-open-source-announcement The ecosystem is still small relative to model sharing on HuggingFace, but it spans hobbyist, research, and commercial deployment, and the supply-chain trust assumption our attack exploits, that a user computing or downloading a vector from upstream-provided contrastive pairs trusts those pairs, is already standard practice in every one of these pipelines.

sections.text: The attack we describe is dual-use: the same procedure that demonstrates the vulnerability can be misused to jailbreak deployed models. We mitigate this in two ways. First, we publish a defense (refusal-direction orthogonalisation, Section 4.7 ) and a complementary cosine-threshold screen ( Appendix E ) that together neutralise the attack on every combo we tested. Second, our threat model targets a community-sharing pipeline that is still small ( Appendix C ); publishing now, before the ecosystem scales, gives maintainers of llama.cpp , repeng , and HuggingFace steering-vector repositories time to add the integrity checks our defense suggests.

sections.heading: Appendix K Theoretical Guarantees
sections.text: The poisoning objective in Equation 3 is a discrete, nonconvex optimization problem over token sequences; we do not claim that Algorithm 1 finds a global optimum. This appendix formalises algorithmic guarantees: the procedure stays inside the stealth-preserving feasible set, monotonically improves the attack objective whenever it accepts an update, and admits a local-optimality interpretation for an exhaustive variant. For the proofs, it is useful to collect all stealth constraints into a single mathematical object: the feasible set of poisoned datasets. This lets us reason about the algorithm as an ascent procedure over a finite constrained search space. We prove three results. First, Algorithm 1 preserves feasibility, monotonically improves the cosine objective whenever it accepts an update, and terminates after finitely many accepted updates. Second, an idealized exhaustive version of the search procedure returns a coordinatewise local optimum whenever it completes a full non-improving sweep. Third, under a Lipschitz assumption on the hidden-state map, the steering-vector perturbation caused by poisoning is explicitly bounded by the edit budget and the embedding radius of the neighbor table.

sections.text: The first result states that the practical algorithm always remains inside the allowed search space and never decreases the attack objective. This is the basic correctness property needed to interpret the method as constrained ascent. Theorem K.6 (Feasibility, monotonicity, and finite termination) . Assume Algorithm 1 is initialized at the original dataset D 0 D_{0} and accepts a candidate only when its cosine objective strictly improves over the current best value. We first prove feasibility. The original dataset is feasible by definition when zero edits are applied. At each iteration, candidate generation only proposes replacements from the precomputed neighbor table, and each neighbor belongs to the safe vocabulary. The algorithm skips edits that would exceed the per-text budget n mod n_{\mathrm{mod}} and never modifies protected suffix positions. By induction over iterations, D t ∈ 𝒟 D_{t}\in\mathcal{D} for all t t . We next prove monotonicity. At iteration t t , either the algorithm accepts a candidate or it does not. sections.heading: Scope of the guarantees.
sections.text: These guarantees should be interpreted as algorithmic guarantees rather than global optimization guarantees. They show that the procedure is a feasible monotone ascent method over a finite constrained search space, and that an exhaustive coordinate-ascent variant has a standard local-optimality property. They do not imply that the returned dataset globally maximizes cos ⁡ ( 𝐯 ⁡ ( D ) , 𝐫 ) \cos(\mathbf{v}(D),\mathbf{r}) over 𝒟 \mathcal{D} .

However, we show that a stealth data poisoning attack silently compromises this pipeline. By substituting 4 − 6 % 4{-}6\% of tokens in the steering dataset, an attacker can silently align the resulting vector with an anti-refusal direction. This jailbreaks the target model while preserving the intended steering effect on benign prompts. Under this threat model, a malicious actor can distribute an apparently safe bundle containing texts, vectors, and weights, alongside an equivalence certificate that the end-user can verify. We test the attack on two open-weight model families and eight model-attribute combinations, observing that poisoned vectors reach an absolute attack success rate (ASR) of 20 − 55 % 20{-}55\% , + 19 % +19\% to + 51 % +51\% over a clean reference. Finally, we find that a refusal-direction orthogonalization defense can recover ≈ 82 % {\approx}82\% of the ASR gap without harming benign behavior. The declared attribute still fires on benign prompts, but refusal is suppressed on harmful ones. Large language models (LLMs) undergo extensive safety alignment to refuse harmful requests, yet adversarial jailbreaks remain a persistent threat. Most existing attacks operate at the prompt level : gradient-based adversarial suffixes ( Zou et al., 2023 ) , automated red-teaming ( Chao et al., 2025 ) , or template-based injections ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Wei et al., 2023 ) . These approaches are visible in the model input and increasingly mitigated by perplexity-based or classifier-based input filters. In parallel, a different paradigm for controlling LLM behavior has gained traction: activation steering ( Turner et al., 2024 ; Zou et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2023 ) . Rather than crafting adversarial prompts, users compute a direction vector from contrastive text pairs, prompts that exhibit a target attribute ( pos ) versus prompts that do not ( neg ), and add this vector to the model’s hidden states at inference time. The technique is simple, requires no fine-tuning, and generalizes across open-weight models ( Rimsky et al., 2024 ) . Because it is lightweight and reusable, activation steering enables a new ecosystem of shared steering datasets and precomputed vectors , in which users have the possibility to download and apply steering artifacts computed by others rather than recomputing them in-house ( Appendix C ). A supply-chain vulnerability. This sharing practice introduces a new trust surface. If a user computes a steering vector from a community-provided contrastive dataset, nothing prevents a malicious contributor from poisoning that dataset. We show that such poisoning can be both effective and stealthy : the attacker makes small token substitutions in the contrastive pair texts, constrained to embedding-space nearest neighbors, so that the resulting steering vector silently aligns with the anti-refusal direction . When applied at inference, the poisoned vector suppresses the model’s safety guardrails. A user who downloads a dataset labeled “bullet list formatting” would unwittingly deploy a jailbreak vector. Crucially, the vulnerability survives strong provenance guarantees: even if the attacker ships a bundle (pair texts, precomputed vector, suggested weight) together with a cryptographic equivalence certificate that the user can re-derive locally, the certificate proves only that the vector was computed correctly from the released texts, and it is the texts that carry the payload. The attack therefore targets a regime that bit-exact reproducibility does not defend against. Why this is possible. The attack exploits a fundamental property of LLM representations: entanglement . The direction encoding a benign attribute (e.g., “use bullet lists”) occupies the same space as the direction mediating refusal ( Arditi et al., 2024 ) ; there is no orthogonality guarantee between them, so small perturbations to the contrastive texts can rotate the steering vector toward 𝐫 \mathbf{r} . Because the vector is a mean-difference of hidden states, each token substitution contributes a small Δ \Delta , and gradient-guided search lets these deltas accumulate into a significant directional shift while each individual change remains imperceptible. What distinguishes our attack. Our approach differs from prior work along three axes. Attack surface: we target the steering dataset , not the inference-time prompt; the adversarial payload is baked into the contrastive pairs before any user touches the model. Stealth: unlike GCG-style suffixes that produce gibberish (perplexity > 1000 {>}1000 ), our replacements are constrained to embedding-space nearest neighbours from a curated safe vocabulary and are dominantly synonym-like swaps ( write → \to describe , short → \to concise , poem → \to poetry ); the optimiser typically modifies only 4–6% of tokens, and the resulting vector still elicits the declared attribute on benign prompts essentially as strongly as the clean vector, with ℓ 2 \ell_{2} norm essentially unchanged on seven of eight combos. Mechanism: the attack manipulates neither model weights, as in training-data poisoning ( Carlini et al., 2024 ; Wan et al., 2023 ) , nor the input, but corrupts a post-hoc representation-level intervention, bypassing both input filters and weight-level audits. Contributions. 1. We identify contrastive steering datasets as a novel attack surface and formalise the supply-chain threat model ( Section 3 ). 2. We propose a GCG-style optimisation constrained to embedding-space neighbours with fluency penalties and safe-vocabulary filtering, producing stealthy poisoned contrastive pairs ( Section 3 ). 3. We validate the attack on two open-weight model families and eight model–attribute combos spanning language, formatting, and case, showing 0.20 0.20 – 0.55 0.55 ASR ( + 19 +19 to + 51 +51 pp over clean) while leaving the declared steering effect on benign prompts and the vector’s ℓ 2 \ell_{2} norm essentially unchanged on seven of eight combos ( Section 4 ). 2 Related Work Activation steering and representation engineering. Turner et al. (2024) introduced Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA): computing mean-difference vectors from contrastive text pairs and adding them to hidden states to steer model behavior. Zou et al. (2025) generalized this into Representation Engineering, a framework for reading and controlling model internals via linear probes and interventions. Rimsky et al. (2024) demonstrated contrastive steering on Llama 2 across a range of behavioral attributes, and Li et al. (2023) applied similar interventions to elicit truthful outputs. Arditi et al. (2024) showed that refusal in LLMs is mediated by a single linear direction, and that ablating this direction eliminates refusal entirely. These works establish the techniques we build on, and the assumptions we exploit. None consider the security of the contrastive dataset used to compute steering vectors. Adversarial attacks on LLMs. Zou et al. (2023) proposed Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG), a gradient-based method that appends adversarial suffixes to prompts, achieving transferable jailbreaks. GCG produces high-perplexity gibberish that is detectable by input filters. Liu et al. (2024) developed AutoDAN, which uses evolutionary search to produce more readable adversarial prompts, and Chao et al. (2025) introduced PAIR, leveraging an attacker LLM to iteratively refine jailbreak prompts. Wei et al. (2023) taxonomized failure modes of LLM safety training, including competing objectives and mismatched generalization. All of these attacks operate at the prompt level at inference time. Our attack is fundamentally different: it corrupts the steering dataset before inference, so the adversarial prompts at test time are clean, unmodified harmful requests. Data poisoning and backdoor attacks. Carlini et al. (2024) demonstrated that poisoning web-scale training datasets is practical. Wan et al. (2023) showed that instruction-tuning data can be poisoned to degrade model safety. Hubinger et al. (2024) trained deceptive “sleeper agent” models that persist through safety training. These attacks target model weights via the training pipeline. Our attack targets a post-hoc representation-level intervention : the model weights are never modified, and the poisoning operates on an auxiliary dataset used solely for steering vector computation. This makes our threat model orthogonal to classical data poisoning. 3 Methodology 3.1 Threat Model We consider an attacker with white-box access to the target model, realistic for open-weight models such as Gemma ( Gemma Team, 2024 ) and Llama ( Llama Team, AI @ Meta, 2024 ) , who distributes a bundle : contrastive pair texts, a precomputed steering vector 𝐯 \mathbf{v} , a recommended steering weight α \alpha , and an equivalence certificate the user can verify by re-deriving 𝐯 \mathbf{v} from the released texts. A user who downloads the bundle (i) re-derives 𝐯 \mathbf{v} to confirm provenance, (ii) reads the pair texts to check they look natural, and (iii) runs a benign sanity check that ( 𝐯 , α ) (\mathbf{v},\alpha) produces the advertised attribute behaviour, and if all three pass deploys at the bundled α \alpha . The cryptographic certificate proves only that 𝐯 \mathbf{v} was correctly computed from the released texts; it does not detect that the texts themselves carry the payload. The attacker’s goal is to modify the dataset so that the resulting steering vector aligns with 𝐫 \mathbf{r} , the anti-refusal direction, suppressing safety guardrails at inference. The attack is subject to a stealth constraint : the poisoned texts must be plausible paraphrases of the originals. We enforce this through (i) a per-text edit budget of at most n mod n_{\text{mod}} token changes, (ii) replacements restricted to embedding-space nearest neighbors, (iii) replacements drawn from a curated safe vocabulary, and (iv) a hard perplexity cap on modified texts. 3.2 Background Contrastive steering vectors. Constraining replacements to embedding-space neighbours from a curated safe vocabulary generates texts that look like minor paraphrases, with the optimiser typically touching only 4–6% of modifiable tokens. Across two model families and eight combinations, poisoned vectors reach 0.20 0.20 – 0.55 0.55 absolute ASR ( + 19 +19 to + 51 +51 pp over the clean counterfactual) while attribute compliance on benign prompts shifts by at most 0.11 0.11 and ℓ 2 \ell_{2} norm stays close to clean on seven of eight combos, so a user who sanity-checks the bundled artefact sees the behaviour the dataset’s label promises, and the jailbreak surfaces only on harmful inputs. Verification of shared steering artefacts must therefore test the artefact on adversarial inputs, not just on the benign queries it was advertised to steer, and not only by re-deriving the vector from the texts. Limitations The attack requires white-box access for gradient computation and embedding-neighbour lookup; this is realistic for open-weight models but does not apply to closed APIs. We test only up to 8B parameters; larger models may have different representational geometry both for 𝐫 \mathbf{r} and for the entanglement we exploit. One combo (Gemma-2-2B lowercase at layer 14) is weakly-steered (clean AC = 0.14 =0.14 at the bundled weight), failing the bundle protocol’s benign sanity check; we retain it for transparency but it does not contribute to the stealth claim. Finally, we only target the refusal direction; other attack objectives and cross-model transferability remain unexplored. We mitigate this in two ways. Second, our threat model targets a community-sharing pipeline that is still small ( Appendix C ); publishing now, before the ecosystem scales, gives maintainers of llama.cpp , repeng , and HuggingFace steering-vector repositories time to add the integrity checks our defense suggests. Appendix J Use of AI Assistants We used LLM coding assistants for refactoring, plotting scripts, and boilerplate, and LLMs for sentence-level prose polishing; all technical content, claims, and experimental design are authored and verified by the authors. LLMs are also used as part of the methodology itself, as evaluation judges ( Section 4 , Appendix F ) and in the safe-vocabulary screening pipeline ( Appendix A ); these uses are described in the body of the paper. Appendix K Theoretical Guarantees The poisoning objective in Equation 3 is a discrete, nonconvex optimization problem over token sequences; we do not claim that Algorithm 1 finds a global optimum. This appendix formalises algorithmic guarantees: the procedure stays inside the stealth-preserving feasible set, monotonically improves the attack objective whenever it accepts an update, and admits a local-optimality interpretation for an exhaustive variant. For the proofs, it is useful to collect all stealth constraints into a single mathematical object: the feasible set of poisoned datasets. This lets us reason about the algorithm as an ascent procedure over a finite constrained search space. We prove three results. First, Algorithm 1 preserves feasibility, monotonically improves the cosine objective whenever it accepts an update, and terminates after finitely many accepted updates. Second, an idealized exhaustive version of the search procedure returns a coordinatewise local optimum whenever it completes a full non-improving sweep. Third, under a Lipschitz assumption on the hidden-state map, the steering-vector perturbation caused by poisoning is explicitly bounded by the edit budget and the embedding radius of the neighbor table.
